Thanks.
Agnieszka and Carla

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Doing partial-f test for netlm models?
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Doing partial-f test for netlm models?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I have been using the statnet package for a while and have worked with
regression analysis off and on.

What I'm trying to do is find how much variance an independent
variable explains by comparing two netlm models: one with Y = B0 +
B1X1 + B2X2 + B3X3 + B4X4 + e and the other  Y = B0 + B1X1 + B2X2 +
B3X3 + e.

I understand that in typical multiple regression I can find the
difference in the adjusted R^2 and then use anova to test if there is
a significant difference between models. Unfortunately, the netlm
object doesn't seem to support this. I get:

> anova(fit.0, fit.1)
Error in UseMethod("anova") :
  no applicable method for 'anova' applied to an object of class "netlm"

Questions:
1) can anyone suggest a manual way to do this?
2) alternately, is there a different approach to get at the same thing?

Thank you.

-- 
Jeff Hemsley
Doctoral Student
The iSchool
University of Washington
http://ischool.uw.edu/
jhemsley@uw.edu

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] latentnet - Backing off: too few acceptances (burnin not long enough)
messages.body_plain:
Dear statnet-community,

I hope someone might help me with a specific issue which causes some bad headache to me. I am doing research on a network consisting of 400 vertices and 2446 edges. The network is directed and has some loops. Additionally, I use one edge-covariate to model the quantity of transfers on the edges. I'd like to find latent clusters in the network.
My script is as follows:
latentnetwork <- ergmm(network ~ latent(d=2, G=1) + latentcov(network, attrname='value'), verbose=TRUE, control=ergmm.control(burnin=50000, sample.size=10000, interval=5))

While the "Burning in"-procedure, I get following message:
"Backing off: too few acceptances. If you see this message several times in a row, use a longer burnin."

I already increased the burnin to 50,000 interations which is five times more than default and I still get the same message fifty times or more in a row.

Has someone some experience how to handle this specific issue. I can't find anything if I google the message.

Thanks.
Sebastian

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Memory increases dramatically with ergm function
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Memory increases dramatically with ergm function
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I have a question regarding ergm memory management. I have a network with
300,000 nodes and about 1,300,000 edges. The network object when loaded
occupies about 1,2 GB of memory. I have 8GB available. My issue is that
when I run the ergm procedure the memory used increases by an additional
3GB(up until fitting initial model stage). Is ergm really that demanding or
am I doing something wrong?

Here is my code for reference. Feel free to give me any suggestions or
optimizing procedures you think is best (I am a newbie with ergm).

usersn = read.table(file =
"file",head=F,sep="\t",comment='',allowEscapes=F,quote="",stringsAsFactors=FALSE)
user = read.table(file =
"file2",head=F,sep="\t",comment='',allowEscapes=F,quote="",stringsAsFactors=FALSE)
usersn = usersn[with(usersn, order(V1)), ]
user = user[with(user, order(V1)), ]
el = usersn[,1:2]
n=network(el,directed=T)
n %v% "score" <- round(user[,6],2)

n01 <- ergm(n ~edges + mutual +
nodecov('score'),verbose=T,control=control.ergm(MCMC.samplesize=70000,MCMLE.maxit
= 10, MCMC.burnin = 20000,seed=25,parallel=7,parallel.type="SOCK",
calc.mcmc.se=F))

Best,
Michael Tsikerdekis

Hi Ken,

Yes, you can, with the terms "odegree" and "idegree", to capture out- or 
in-degree, respectively.

Cheers,
Steve


PS In general, a good place to find info on the various terms available 
is with:

?"ergm-terms"

We've tried to include some cross-references among terms in there to 
help folks find other terms (including the case of degree and its 
directed forms). That said, even with those tips there are all kinds of 
cases where it's hard to find the term one may be interested--and the 
listserv is indeed another good place to turn for help, as you've found.

               Florentine.Marriage.Adj<-graph.adjacency(Florentine.Marriage,mode="directed",weighted=NULL,diag=FALSE,add.colnames=NULL,add.rownames=NULL)

messages.subject: [statnet_help] MCMC standard errors
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

(Happy summer!)

I have a couple quick questions I'm hoping one of the developers can answer- the first of which I believe was posted a couple times last year, but I couldn't find a response in the archives or a clear answer in the documentation (apologies if I missed it!).

1. The ergm command currently provides as part of the output "MCMC %." Can someone explain precisely what this means? (i.e. I understand that there are two components to the standard error when using MCMC- so does the percentage refer to the proportion of the reported SE that is due to the MCMC process- and therefore the reported SE's and p-values already reflect both types of SE's- or is it an extra percentage that should somehow be "added on"?) Additionally, is there any guidance for how big we should usually expect these %'s to be, or techniques to minimize them? (Other than the standard recommendations in the documentation for improving convergence.)

2. For some reason, whenever I run a model that includes a coefficient that cannot be estimated (for instance, let's say I am modeling an academic network and I include a nodematch term for sociologists, but there are no ties between sociologists so the parameter is fixed at "-Inf"), all of my MCMC %'s appear as "NA" instead of an actual number. Is there a reason for this; and should I be concerned about it? E.g. does this mean that the reported SE's are not conservative enough because they don't incorporate the extra MCMC SE?

Thanks in advance for any guidance!

-Kevin

Kevin Lewis
Assistant Professor of Sociology
University of California, San Diego

messages.subject: [statnet_help] MCMC standard errors
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Kevin,

> 1. The ergm command currently provides as part of the output ?MCMC %.?
> Can someone explain precisely what this means? (i.e. I understand that
> there are two components to the standard error when using MCMC- so does
> the percentage refer to the proportion of the reported SE that is due to
> the MCMC process- and therefore the reported SE?s and p-values already
> reflect both types of SE?s- or is it an extra percentage that should
> somehow be ?added on??)

The SE reported includes the MCMC error, and the percentage is the 
percentage of the *variance* due to MCMC: SEmcmc^2 / (SEmcmc^2 + 
SEmodel^2) * 100%.

> Additionally, is there any guidance for how big
> we should usually expect these %?s to be, or techniques to minimize
> them? (Other than the standard recommendations in the documentation for
> improving convergence.)

Other than the standard recommendations --- increase MCMC sample size 
and/or interval, write a better MCMC sampler, etc. --- I don't have any.

> 2. For some reason, whenever I run a model that includes a coefficient
> that cannot be estimated (for instance, let?s say I am modeling an
> academic network and I include a nodematch term for sociologists, but
> there are no ties between sociologists so the parameter is fixed at
> ?-Inf?), all of my MCMC %?s appear as ?NA? instead of an actual number.
> Is there a reason for this; and should I be concerned about it? E.g.
> does this mean that the reported SE?s are not conservative enough
> because they don?t incorporate the extra MCMC SE?

No, this is a long-standing bug in a rather involved part of ergm, where 
models with any offset terms (not just the +-Inf ones from dropping) 
broke the MCMC SE calculation. Having taken another look, I think I know 
how to fix it, though, so we'll probably have it working in the next 
release.

                   I hope this helps,
                   Pavel
